name: Tree Pollen
description: Tree pollen is one of the most common causes of seasonal allergies. Trees begin releasing pollen in early spring, sometimes as early as February in southern states. Oak, birch, cedar, and maple are among the most problematic species.
prevention: Keep windows closed during peak season

name: Grass Pollen
description: Grass pollen is the primary allergen from late spring through summer. Timothy grass, Kentucky bluegrass, Bermuda grass, and ryegrass are common culprits. Agricultural regions have particularly high grass pollen counts.
prevention: Stay indoors on high count days

name: Weed Pollen
description: Weed pollen dominates the fall allergy season. Ragweed is the most notorious weed allergen, producing billions of pollen grains per plant. Other problematic weeds include mugwort, lamb's quarters, and pigweed.

name: Ragweed
description: Ragweed is the most significant allergy trigger in North America. A single plant can produce up to one billion pollen grains. Its pollen can travel hundreds of miles on the wind. About 75% of people with plant allergies are allergic to ragweed.

name: Oak Pollen
description: Oak trees are one of the longest and heaviest pollen producers among trees. Oak pollen season can last from February through May depending on location. Oak trees are ubiquitous across the eastern United States, making this allergen hard to avoid.
prevention: Keep car and home windows closed

name: Birch Pollen
description: Birch pollen is a major allergen in northern climates. It's also cross-reactive with many foods including apples, cherries, peaches, hazelnuts, and carrots. About 25% of pollen allergy sufferers are sensitive to birch pollen.

name: Cedar / Juniper Pollen
description: Mountain cedar (Ashe juniper) causes 'cedar fever' in Texas from December through February. It's one of the most intense allergy seasons anywhere in the United States, with pollen counts often reaching extreme levels. Symptoms can mimic the flu.
prevention: Stock up on antihistamines in November
Run air conditioning instead of opening windows

name: Maple Pollen
description: Maple trees are among the earliest spring pollinators, beginning to release pollen while snow is still on the ground in some regions. Box elder, a type of maple, is particularly prolific. Maple allergies can overlap with other early spring allergens.
prevention: Prepare allergy medications in late winter
Keep windows closed on warm early spring days

name: Mold Spores
description: Mold spores are present year-round but peak in warm, humid conditions. Outdoor mold grows on decaying leaves, compost, and soil. Indoor mold can grow in damp areas. Alternaria and Cladosporium are the most common outdoor mold allergens.

name: Timothy Grass Pollen
description: Timothy grass is one of the most common grasses in North America and a major source of grass allergies. It's widely planted as hay for livestock. Timothy grass allergy is so common it's used as a reference standard in allergy testing.

name: Bermuda Grass Pollen
description: Bermuda grass is one of the most allergenic grasses in the southern United States, producing pollen from spring through fall in warm climates. It's widely used in lawns and sports fields throughout the Sun Belt states.
prevention: Replace Bermuda grass with low-allergen alternatives
Wear gloves and mask when mowing

name: Mugwort Pollen
description: Mugwort is a common roadside weed that's a significant allergen in both North America and Europe. It's cross-reactive with many foods including celery, carrots, spices, and some fruits — a condition known as Mugwort-celery syndrome.

name: Pine Pollen
description: Pine pollen is produced in enormous quantities and is often visible as yellow dust coating surfaces. Despite being alarming in appearance, pine pollen grains are relatively large and don't penetrate the nasal passages as easily as smaller pollen grains. Pine allergy is less common than other tree allergies.
prevention: Rinse outdoor surfaces during pine season
Monitor pollen counts even if symptoms are mild

name: Alder Pollen
description: Alder trees are among the very first trees to release pollen in late winter and early spring. They're common in the Pacific Northwest and are a major allergen in that region. Alder pollen is cross-reactive with birch pollen and hazel.

name: Elm Pollen
description: Elm trees pollinate very early in spring, often before leaves appear. They're common street and shade trees in many American cities. Elm allergy can be severe and often catches people off guard because symptoms start while weather is still cold.
prevention: Start allergy medications in late winter
Avoid planting elm trees near homes
